label: Weight–length coefficient k = W/L³ is constant iff the animal's form is unchanged
notation: W = kL^3; form unchanged during growth \iff k constant
assumptions: Weight W = ρ · c L³ with constant nonzero density ρ and shape factor c(t) standing for the general form; length nonzero.
scope_note: Proves k = ρc, so k is constant over growth iff the shape factor is. Whether real fishes change form while growing is left to data.

label: Greenhill: a self-supporting column's diameter must grow as height^{3/2}
notation: d \propto h^{3/2} (no buckling under own weight); h_{max} \approx 300\,\text{ft} for the Kew-flagstaff pine
assumptions: Greenhill's critical-height law h_crit = C d^{2/3}, with C > 0 bundling stiffness, density, gravity and the taper/branching assumptions; d, h ≥ 0.
scope_note: Takes Greenhill's buckling result h_crit ∝ d^{2/3} as the definition (the elastic-stability derivation is not formalized) and proves that standing requires d ≥ (h/C)^{3/2}, with the minimum diameter scaling as λ^{3/2} when height scales by λ. The 300 ft limit for the Kew pine depends on measured material constants and is not proved.

label: Strength-to-weight ratio falls as 1/L, bounding the size of animals under gravity
notation: strength \propto L^2, W \propto L^3 \Rightarrow strength/W \propto L^{-1}, so L is bounded above under gravity
assumptions: Strength proportional to cross-section (a L²), weight to volume (b L³), with fixed shape; b, L > 0; supporting the body requires strength/weight ≥ r > 0.
scope_note: Proves strength/weight = (a/b)/L and that a required ratio r caps size at L ≤ a/(b r). The elephant being near the limit, and whether real strength scales as L², are empirical.

label: Muscular capacity ∝ L³ outgrows respiratory supply ∝ L², favouring large-animal spurts
assumptions: Muscular (burst) capacity a L³ and energy-supply rate b L² for similar animals; a, b > 0; 0 < L₁ < L₂.
scope_note: Proves the capacity-to-supply ratio grows linearly in L and that a larger animal's burst advantage (L₂/L₁)³ exceeds its sustained-supply advantage (L₂/L₁)². The predictions about equal yearly distance, fatigue curves and staying power are not derived from these scalings alone and are left to observation.

label: Flight work ∝ L^{7/2} vs muscle work ∝ L³: flight ~1.4× harder per doubling of size
notation: V_{min} \propto L^{1/2}; W_{flight} = mV^2 \propto L^{7/2}; W_{muscle} \propto L^3; per doubling of L: 2^{7/2} : 2^3 \approx 1.4 : 1
assumptions: Thompson's equations: weight c₁ l³ balanced by momentum m V of downthrust air with m = c₂ l² V; flight work m V²; muscular work μ l³; all constants and l positive.
scope_note: Proves V = √((c₁/c₂) l), W² = c² k³ l⁷ (W ∝ l^{7/2}), that doubling l multiplies W by 2³√2, and that required/available work rises by √2 ∈ (1.4, 1.42) per doubling. Real birds' aerodynamics beyond Thompson's momentum model are not addressed.

label: Borelli's law: similarly built animals jump to the same actual height
notation: impulse \propto M \Rightarrow v_0 independent of L; jump height h = v_0^2/2g independent of L
assumptions: Take-off velocity v₀ = x/M and ballistic height v₀²/2g; impulse x = β M (proportional to muscle volume, hence body mass); M ≠ 0.
scope_note: Proves the jump height β²/2g is independent of mass, so any two sizes jump equally high. The advantage of longer levers in larger animals and actual jump data are not modelled.

label: Swimming, flight and pendulum walking all give velocity ∝ √(linear size)
notation: V \propto L^{1/2} for swimming (Froude), flight (minimum speed) and walking (pendulum leg)
assumptions: Swimming at a fixed Froude number V = Fr √(gL); flight speed from the momentum balance V = √(k L); walking with stride a L per pendulum period 2π√(L/g); g > 0, k ≥ 0.
scope_note: Proves each of the three speed laws has the form C √L for all L > 0. Differences in mechanical construction (lever use, bent legs in running) that Thompson sets aside are not modelled.

label: Constant surface-to-mass ratio requires a change of form growing with size
notation: S/M \approx \text{const} maintained by change of form, against S/M \propto L^{-1} for similar forms
assumptions: Surface σ L² with σ a surface (folding) factor, mass ρ c L³; ρ, c, L nonzero.
scope_note: Proves S/M ∝ 1/L for similar forms and that S/M = κ holds iff σ = κ ρ c L, i.e. the folding factor must grow in proportion to size. That villi, spiral valves and brain convolutions actually do this is the empirical part.

label: Cell division raises total surface by n^{1/3} at fixed volume, restoring S/V
notation: cell division keeps S/M \approx \text{const}; cleavage increases S at constant V and M
assumptions: Cells modelled as spheres, surface (36π)^{1/3} V^{2/3}; division into n equal spheres at unchanged total volume; V > 0.
scope_note: Proves division into n spheres multiplies total surface by n^{1/3} (strictly more for n > 1), and that a cell that doubled its volume and divides restores the daughters' S/V to the original. The surface-energy balance and the mechanism triggering division are not formalized.

label: Weight varies as the cube of length whatever the law of linear growth
notation: W \propto L^3 whatever the law of growth L(t)
assumptions: Fixed form and density, W = k L³ with k ≠ 0; arbitrary length curve L(t), differentiable where the rate is taken.
scope_note: Proves W(t)/W(s) = (L(t)/L(s))³ for any growth law and dW/dt = 3kL² dL/dt, so the weight curve's shape differs from the stature curve. The part not explained by the cube law (changes of form and density in humans) is empirical.

label: Plaice weight–length coefficient k rises to a maximum near 30 cm, then declines
notation: k = W/L^3 not constant in plaice; \max_L k at L \approx 30\,\text{cm}
reason: Purely empirical: the shape of k(L) and the location of its maximum come from plaice measurements. The definition k = W/L³ is already formalized as weightCoeff for thompson1917-ch02-01; nothing further can be proved without data.

label: Van 't Hoff's law: a rise of n degrees multiplies growth rate by xⁿ
notation: v(\theta + n) = x^n v(\theta) for a rise of n degrees; temperature coefficient of growth x^{10} \approx 2\text{--}3
assumptions: Rate v(θ) = v₀ x^θ with per-degree coefficient x > 0, within the normal temperature range; v₀ ≠ 0.
scope_note: Proves v(θ + n) = xⁿ v(θ) and that the ten-degree coefficient is x^{10}. That growth follows this law, and the value 2–3 per 10 °C, are empirical.

label: Seasonal growth as a damped annual sine curve that fades as growth slows
notation: L(t) = \bar{L}(t) + A(t)\sin(2\pi t / 1\,\text{yr}), A(t) \to 0 as d\bar{L}/dt \to 0 (damped sine)
assumptions: Length L̄(t) + A(t) sin(2πt) with t in years; amplitude proportional to the growth rate, A(t) = c r(t), with r(t) → 0.
scope_note: Proves the seasonal term has a one-year period and that the deviation from the mean curve tends to 0 as the growth rate does. That plaice, haddock and humans grow this way is empirical.

label: Regenerative growth velocity falls as an inverse power of time, V T² ≈ const
notation: V^m T^n = \text{const}; for regenerating tadpole tails V T^2 \approx \text{const}
assumptions: V^m T^n = K with V, T > 0 and m ≠ 0; for tadpole tails m = 1, n = 2, V = C/T² with C > 0.
scope_note: Proves the family is linear in log coordinates, log V = (log K − n log T)/m, that V = C/T² is its m = 1, n = 2 member, and that V decreases with T. That tadpole-tail data fit n/m ≈ 2 is empirical.
